1:
The vision continues from where it broke off. Gill has the prophet lifted from the inner court by the same Spirit that had once taken him by a lock of his head, perhaps in the same manner; Ellicott traces the movement more exactly, from the court of the priests to the main outer entrance of the whole enclosure, the very place to which he had watched the cherubim go, so that the vision runs consecutively. Keil and Delitzsch render the agent a wind and set out what follows in three parts: the destruction of the ungodly rulers, the promise that the Lord would gather a people out of the exiles and sanctify them by his Spirit, and the withdrawal of his presence from the city with the prophet's return to Chaldea. Clarke divides it the same way.

Whether the twenty-five men are the twenty-five already seen is disputed. Clarke has no doubt they are the same persons who had been worshipping the sun. Henry is equally sure they are not: those stood between the porch and the altar and were priests or Levites, while these sit in the gate to try causes, and are charged not with corrupt worship but with maladministration. Ellicott reports that they are generally supposed different, the one set priestly and the other secular, but will not close the question, since it is not impossible that the same idolatrous priests, having prostituted their office, had gained an ascendancy over the people.

The number itself is read three ways. Ellicott offers the king with two princes from each of the twelve tribes, or else no significance beyond a considerable array of the most prominent men. Henry reports that some divided the city into twenty-four wards and made these the governors of them with their president. Calvin declines all such arithmetic: a definite number is put for an indefinite, and what matters is only that those who held the reins of government were despisers of God, so that it is no wonder the defection spread through the whole people.

The two names are handled for their meaning and their sequel. Clarke notes that a Jaazaniah has already appeared as the son of Shaphan, allows that the two might be one man if Shaphan was also called Azur, but thinks it likelier there were two of the name, both chiefs. Henry and Wesley both keep them separate, and Wesley adds that Pelatiah is named here for the sake of the sudden death that made him a warning. Ellicott presses the etymologies, the Lord hears, the helper, God rescues, the Lord builds, and takes them as chosen to bring out the false hopes the people beguiled themselves with, which is what made that death so impressive.

The charge is that they devise mischief. Henry reads the counsel as advice to silence the prophets, rebel against the king of Babylon and hold the city to the last extremity, all of it offered under pretence of concerting measures for the public safety, and observes that it goes badly with a people when the things belonging to their peace are hidden from those entrusted with their counsels. Calvin makes the leaders the cause of the ruin outright, since if the blind lead the blind both fall into the ditch; and he adds the reason the point had to be made, that ordinary men treat their rulers as a shield and think themselves guilty of nothing so long as they obeyed, throwing off all blame under pretence of ignorance. He notes too what the accusation costs the prophet, who attacks the noblest men in the city without sparing them. From this he draws the standing lesson that rank confers no immunity, that no eminence is sacred or absolved from law, and that whoever teaches must put away all respect of persons.
3:
What the princes mean by it is not near is disputed at the level of the words. Clarke takes the plain sense, the threatened invasion. Gill agrees, but records two other renderings the Hebrew will bear, that it is not proper to build near the city where the enemy would destroy the houses, or not to build inside it for the crowds fleeing in, who would exhaust the provisions. He objects to both as prudent advice rather than wicked counsel. Ellicott says neither text nor margin renders the original accurately: it is literally not near to build houses, and it is a retort. The exiles had been told by letter to build, because the captivity would be long, which so offended them that a false prophet among them wrote to Jerusalem demanding the writer be punished. The princes take up that word and deny it.

The caldron is their own figure and a scoff. Ellicott has them comparing the city to a pot whose strong walls keep the flesh inside safe from the fire of attack. Clarke allows two readings of the jest: a resolve to share the city's fate, or ridicule of the earlier vision of a seething pot, that they were to have been boiled long ago and it has not happened yet. Calvin develops the ridicule furthest. They pretended to find an inconsistency: if the city is the pot and they the flesh, they are meant to stay in it, so the threat of exile contradicts the figure. They granted they might be lightly scorched, but expected to live to a good old age. Wesley calls it an impious scoff with some fear in it.

The reply turns the figure. Calvin has the prophet answer jest with jest while striking a mortal wound: the city is already full of slaughter, the pot full and the flesh cooked, and no room left; what remains is that they be cast out as foul flesh for which no pot can be found, consumed not in the city but stretched at full length on the ground. Ellicott puts it without the wit: the strong city would secure only the dead who fell by their violence, while the living who trusted its walls are brought out and handed to the stranger. Clarke says they shall not be allowed to stay and share its fate; Wesley, that being brought forth is wrath, not mercy.

Whose slain they are is answered at three widths. Gill counts the prophets they killed, the blood they shed and the men condemned without cause, and adds all who died in the siege, since these were owing to the advice to hold out. Wesley says the same briefly: they must answer for everyone the Chaldeans killed, having persuaded them to stand out. Calvin widens it past killing: the phrase need not mean men were openly put to death, but embraces every form of injustice, since God reckons as homicides those who oppress the wretched and overturn their fortunes, so the charge holds where no court could convict. Ellicott observes that violence, like licentiousness, is the fruit of defection.

Both mark the Spirit falling afresh. Gill takes it as a renewed illumination showing the prophet what was coming and giving him courage to declare it, the Targum reading it of the spirit of prophecy. Calvin draws a rule from it: though the man was already endued with the gift, the grace had to be renewed at every exercise of it, since one illumination is not enough unless God works daily. The point of insisting on it is that the words are dictated and not his own; and it is why the threat lands where it does, since men who look for a stage on which to argue their case must appear instead in a court where God is the only judge and no cleverness is admitted.
8:
The sentence is read as a sequence rather than a single stroke. Ellicott counts three stages: first the sword they had feared; then expulsion from the city they trusted and delivery into the hands of strangers; and last, what would be most terrible to a Jew, arraignment in the border, at the very edge of the land or outside it. He points to the historical fulfilment, the general carrying the people after the capture to the king at Riblah on the northern confines, where the king's sons were killed before their father's eyes, many others executed, and the father blinded and carried off. By all of it, he adds, they were brought to acknowledge the Lord, not by repenting but by undergoing the judgments. Clarke and Wesley both fix on the same place and explain the phrase geographically, that Riblah lay in Syria but on the very frontier. Clarke adds that the strangers into whose hands they are delivered means chiefly the royal family, and Wesley that the judgment will pursue them wherever they fly and that heavier sufferings are reserved in a strange land.

Gill keeps the caldron running through the whole passage. They are brought out of the very city they had called their pot and thought themselves safe in, and the repetition is there to make the thing certain and to break their vain confidence; they fall by the sword not inside the walls but outside them, when the city was broken up and they fled; and the city is indeed a caldron, only not theirs, being a caldron for the dead and not for the living.

Calvin meets the objection the figure invites. If they are drawn out of the city, does the earlier prophecy about the boiling pot fail? No, he answers, since the Chaldeans would consume them wherever they were; and the cavil is childish, because God never restricted his wrath to one kind of punishment, and the prophets set his judgments out in various ways and under various figures. He notes the manner too, that they are brought into an open plain where they can be killed more easily, and that being dragged out of the city where they thought they had a quiet nest was itself the judgment, before any sword fell.

Whether Pelatiah actually died at that moment divides them. Clarke thinks he was most probably struck dead the very hour the prophet spoke, and compares the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira. Calvin has no doubt he died at the time of the vision, though he allows the man may have died at his own house rather than at the temple threshold, since a vision is not limited to places. Wesley reads it the other way: the thing was done now in vision only, as the slaying of the elders had been earlier, and served as an assurance that when the prophecy was published it would be done in fact.

The outcry is explained by who the man was. Ellicott identifies him as one of the princes already named as devising mischief, and notes that the prophet, greatly affected, turns at once to intercession that God will not make a full end of the remnant. Calvin makes more of the reputation: Pelatiah excelled the other elders and most people thought the stability of the city rested on his counsel, so his fall was a prelude and a presage of the general destruction. He adds two things about the outcry itself, that the prophet is not speaking here out of prophetic knowledge but according to the common opinion, and that the name plays into it, since the root means to escape and gives the word for survivors, so that the very man whose name held out escape is the one taken.
14:
The word that comes next is an answer, not a new beginning. Ellicott insists on that, and on how completely it turns: the denunciations were aimed at Jerusalem, for whom intercession was useless; this reply leaves the city for the exiles. Gill takes it as the answer to the prayer. Calvin reads a rebuke into it. The prophet had cried out at one man's death as though all were lost, and the reply is that when the conspicuous are taken away the Church does not perish with them, since God keeps it by hidden means and not in the pomp men look for; the remnant is to be sought among ordinary and despised men.

The brethren are named twice, and the second phrase is technical. Gill and Henry both render it men of thy redemption, the next of kin on whom the right of redeeming an alienated possession fell, and Henry presses the irony that these kinsmen could redeem nothing, being captives themselves. Ellicott makes the same allusion to the kinsman whose office was to help his ruined relative, and adds that the exiles are then called the whole house of Israel, so the cast-out are the others. Gill notes that the Greek translators mistook the word and gave men of thy captivity, followed by the Syriac and Arabic, and reports Kimchi's view that the three phrases point to three deportations. Wesley alone takes the brethren to be the kindred left behind in the city.

What the city said is quoted with its logic intact. Clarke gives it flatly: go far from the Lord, the land is ours, we shall never be removed and you shall never return. Ellicott fills in the grounds they claimed: they were holier, held the chosen city, the temple, the priesthood and the sacrifices, and possessed the land; the others were outcasts. Henry says they cut them off from membership. Calvin will not read the opening words as a command but as a statement of what suited them, that while those men stay far from the sanctuary the inheritance remains here; and he shows what the boast was worth, their own king being already treated with ignominy and the siege about to reduce mothers to eating their children.

Calvin turns this into his main lesson. The exiles they despised included the prophet himself and the man whose piety Jerusalem had owned as the ornament of the age; and their exile, the penalty of crimes no worse than those of the men who stayed, gave the stayers no standing to disown them. From this he draws the rule not to measure the Church by common opinion or visible splendour, since men are drawn to ruin under the name of a church wherever the show is grand enough, while others despair because they cannot point to one with a finger. The Church is often preserved in hiding places, its members ordinary people of no estimation in the world.

A little sanctuary is the grammatical dispute here. Wesley takes little as size, a small sanctuary against the great temple, to which they may flee as a man flees to the horns of the altar, having in captivity the communion supposed possible only in the house. Ellicott denies the adjective: the word is adverbial and may refer to time or degree, and the connection settles it as time, a sanctuary for a little while, for the term of the captivity, God's presence standing in place of the symbol he had abandoned. Calvin allows either a small sanctuary or a sanctuary of the few who were really his, preferring the first for the contrast between visible splendour and a hidden grace the conquerors trampled and the men at home despised; he compares the psalm calling God a dwelling place from of old, before there was any temple. Clarke keeps it simple: exiled, they are not forgotten.
17:
The gathering is the proof that the sanctuary promise was not empty. Calvin puts it as an objection answered: if the exile were perpetual, the assurance of a hidden sanctuary might seem a deception, so God names its result, the return, and with it the covenant he had interrupted for a short time but never cancelled, having given the land to the patriarch and his seed for ever. Ellicott sets the gift against the boast of the men in the city: they claimed the land as theirs alone, and they will be cast out while the exiles they despised inherit it. He compares the generation that refused to go up, feared their children would be a prey, and was told the children would have the land and they would not.

What the returned exiles do first is remove the abominations. Calvin notes where the reproach falls: not on the idols of the nations but on a people who defiled a land dedicated to God, so the expulsion was the penalty of a sacrilege. He draws two rules from it: blessings are rightly enjoyed only when bent towards pure worship, and no duty is discharged while worship is left mixed, since many corrupt whatever obedience they offer, as though half an allegiance would content God. Ellicott finds the promise fulfilled in the abhorrence in which idolatry was afterwards held, and notes that the pronoun shifts from you to they, which may quietly mean the work belonged to the children rather than the men addressed. Wesley alone keeps the promise on the ground, of those who came back on the proclamations of two Persian kings and cleansed the temple of superstition.

The one heart is taken as unity in two senses. Gill lists both: a heart no longer divided between God and idols, nor double and hypocritical; and concord, an oneness of affection and judgment, so that they are of one heart and one soul. He records that the Greek and Arabic read another heart. Ellicott makes unity of purpose at once consequence and condition of the moral change, since self-will divides and submission does not, and points to a parallel promise of one heart and one way, realised in the early church. Clarke sums it as a system of renewed affections with a new spirit to direct them.

The stone and the flesh are a figure of fitness. Ellicott observes that the phrasing belongs to this prophet, and that the stone stands for what is unnatural and incongruous in a man, to be taken away and replaced by a heart an appeal can move; the effect is obedience, and through it the covenant relation realised. Clarke reads it as a matter of impressions, the one refusing them and the other able to receive and keep them. Wesley calls the stony heart hard, inflexible and incorrigible.

The passage is guarded at both ends. Calvin warns against reading the zeal as the people's own achievement: they could not leave their sins until renewed and born again, and two things must be held together, that the elect attend strenuously to their duty and that they are nothing of themselves. Gill says the same of the walking, that there is neither will nor power for it until the new heart is given; Clarke, that the holiness of the life proves the work upon the heart. At the other stands the recompense of those who do not change. Ellicott sets it against the mercy just promised and refuses to make that promise universal, since responsibility and the power of choice are not taken away, and grace refused leaves a man worse rather than untouched; the heart of their detestable things he calls a figure, the abstract put concretely. Clarke says such men will have what their idols can give; Wesley extends it to any who secretly adhere to idols or provide for their service.
22:
The departure is slow on purpose. Clarke counts the stages and calls the vision a proof of long-suffering: God did not abandon the people at once but left by little and little, first the temple, then the city gate, then the mountain on the east, where he waited to see whether they would turn, and last heaven. Henry gives the reason for the pauses, that the glory found none to intercede and none to invite its return; it went gradually because God left with reluctance and would not have gone had they not forced him. Wesley says the mountain kept him within call, ready to return if even now they would understand the things that made for their peace. Gill notes that the glory, having left the temple, now leaves the city too, and that the prophet was carried off only when all that was needed for the reproof of the one party and the comfort of the other had been shown him.

Why that particular mountain draws two answers. Henry finds an irony in the place: they had set their idols there to confront God in his own house, so that it was called the mount of corruption, and he now pitches his tribunal on it to face the men who thought to keep the temple for themselves. Ellicott takes the geography plainly, a hill higher than the city and overlooking it entirely, and lists what else belongs to it: a later prophet sets the Lord standing there in the day of judgment; there the incarnate Son foretold the second destruction, which Henry also notes; and from it he ascended. On the previous verse he adds that wheels and cherubim move by one impulse.

Calvin takes up the difficulty the departure creates. The people had persuaded themselves God was held captive among them and grew licentious on it; the vision shows he was never so bound, and that he has gone and the house is stripped. That was near incredible, since he had promised to dwell there for ever. But an interruption is no broken promise: the exile had a term, the worship was restored at its end, and so he departed while the place stayed sacred. He adds why the glory is borne above the cherubim: a people governed by outward symbols could not otherwise be persuaded God might be parted from the ark.

The carrying back is evidence that the whole was vision. Calvin insists it was divinely presented and no empty spectre, and holds the prophet never left his place, though he will not press it on anyone who thinks otherwise. Spirit stands opposed to nature: ordinary sight is stopped by the least obstacle, while under the Spirit's light a new faculty works that is not to be measured naturally. The man had been carried out of himself as in an ecstasy and is returned to his ordinary state; and since vision is opposed to reality, being brought back by vision proves he was never bodily in the city.

Why he reports it to his fellow exiles is a question Calvin raises against himself. The lesson seems meant for the people at home, so the telling looks superfluous; but he had a hard contest with the exiles too. Those at home laughed at the captives, while the captives, exposed to every reproach and used servilely, resented bearing with prophets at all, so the warning was as necessary there as here. Calvin also notes the word chosen: the prophet reports what he was shown rather than told, improper for speech but exact here, since God had set the thing before his eyes. Ellicott says the telling was to show the vanity of trusting that the guilty city would be preserved; Clarke, that at first they profited little by it, for which he reproves them sharply.
